questions.question: What is HTML accessibility and why does it matter? It is the practice of writing HTML so everyone — including users of assistive tech — can perceive, operate, and understand your UI, and it's a legal and ethical requirement.
questions.title: HTML Accessibility Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: HTML accessibility (a11y) is the practice of writing HTML and UI so that everyone — including users of assistive technologies like screen readers, keyboard-only users, and people with visual or motor impairments — can perceive, operate, and understand the interface. It exists because the web is a public good and many users don't navigate by mouse or sight; accessible HTML (semantic elements, ARIA, labels, keyboard support, contrast) makes the UI usable for them, and it's both a legal requirement (WCAG, ADA) and an ethical one. Accessibility is also good engineering: semantic HTML improves SEO, robustness, and often code quality.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand a11y as semantic HTML + ARIA + keyboard + contrast (the WCAG pillars) and can name concrete techniques — not just 'add alt text'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reducing a11y to 'add alt text' — missing semantic HTML, ARIA roles/labels, keyboard navigation, focus management, and contrast, which are the bulk of real a11y work.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame a11y around the WCAG principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) and name concrete techniques: semantic HTML, ARIA, keyboard, focus, contrast — it's legal, ethical, and good engineering.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: HTML accessibility (a11y) is the practice of writing HTML and UI so that everyone — including users of assistive technologies like screen readers, keyboard-only users, and people with visual or motor impairments — can perceive, operate, and understand the interface. It exists because the web is a public good and many users don't navigate by mouse or sight; accessible HTML (semantic elements, ARIA, labels, keyboard support, contrast) makes the UI usable for them, and it's both a legal requirement (WCAG, ADA) and an ethical one. Accessibility is also good engineering: semantic HTML improves SEO, robustness, and often code quality. The framework is the WCAG principles — perceivable, operable, understandable, robust (POUR).

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) WCAG POUR — content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust; (2) semantic HTML — use elements for their meaning (button, nav, main, article, header, footer) rather than divs; semantic elements expose their role to assistive tech automatically; (3) ARIA — when HTML isn't enough, ARIA (roles, aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-live) adds semantics; the first rule of ARIA is 'don't use it if a native element works'; (4) keyboard accessibility — every interaction reachable and operable by keyboard; focus order and visible focus; (5) labels and names — form controls have associated labels; images have alt; links and buttons have accessible names; (6) contrast — text/background contrast meets WCAG AA (4.5:1) or AAA (7:1); (7) dynamic content — aria-live for announcements; focus management on route changes and modals.

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is native HTML versus ARIA: the first rule of ARIA is 'if a native HTML element works, use it instead' — a real button is keyboard-accessible and role-exposed for free, while a div+ARIA+tabindex+keydown is error-prone. A second tension: a11y can feel like an add-on, but it's cheapest built in from the start (semantic HTML is free) and most expensive bolted on later (retrofitting ARIA and keyboard support is hard). The third: contrast and motion requirements can conflict with design — the resolution is to design for the requirements (4.5:1 contrast, reduced-motion support) rather than against them.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Accessibility (a11y) means everyone — including screen-reader and keyboard users — can perceive, operate, and understand the UI; it's a legal (WCAG/ADA) and ethical requirement.
WCAG POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust — the four principles.
Semantic HTML (button, nav, main, article) exposes roles and keyboard support for free — prefer it over div+ARIA.
ARIA adds semantics when HTML isn't enough; the first rule is 'don't use ARIA if a native element works'.
Keyboard accessibility and focus management (trap in modal, restore on close) are essential — mouse-only interactions fail many users.
Alt text, labels, and contrast (>=4.5:1 for AA) are the perceivable-pillar basics; build a11y in from the start, not bolted on.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: HTML accessibility is the practice of writing HTML and UI so that everyone — including users of assistive technologies like screen readers, keyboard-only users, and people with visual or motor impairments — can perceive, operate, and understand the interface. It exists because the web is a public good and many users don't navigate by mouse or sight, and accessible HTML makes the UI usable for them — it's both a legal requirement under WCAG and ADA and an ethical one. The framework is the WCAG principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust. The technique I stress first is semantic HTML — using elements like button, nav, main, and article for their meaning, because they expose their role and keyboard support to assistive tech for free, whereas a div with an onClick handler has no role, no keyboard support, and no focus. The first rule of ARIA is that if a native element works, use it instead — ARIA adds semantics when HTML isn't enough, like aria-label, role, and aria-live for dynamic announcements, but a real button beats a div with ARIA every time. Keyboard accessibility and focus management are essential — every interaction must be reachable and operable by keyboard, and modals must trap focus inside and restore it on close. And the perceivable-pillar basics are alt text on images, labels on form controls, and color contrast of at least 4.5-to-1 for WCAG AA. The honest tension is that a11y can feel like an add-on, but it's cheapest built in from the start with semantic HTML and most expensive bolted on later.

followup_questions: What are the four WCAG principles (POUR), and what does each require?
Why is a native <button> more accessible than a <div> with onClick?
What is the first rule of ARIA, and when should you use it?
How do you make a modal accessible (focus trap, restore, aria-modal)?
What is the WCAG AA contrast requirement, and why does it matter?

questions.question: What HTML5 input types and validation attributes are available? Give examples.
questions.title: HTML5 Input Types & Validation Attributes — Complete Reference
questions.direct_answer:
What HTML5 input types and validation attributes are available? Give examples.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser pipeline, framework hooks, and user-visible outcomes), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Input types (email, url, number, tel, date, color, range, search, file) and attributes (required, pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength).

**Classic weak answer:** Relying solely on HTML5 validation — it must be duplicated server-side; client validation is UX-only.

**Senior finish:** Show how :invalid/:valid CSS and the Constraint Validation API (setCustomValidity) let you customize error UX.

interviewer_intent.testing: Input types (email, url, number, tel, date, color, range, search, file) and attributes (required, pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying solely on HTML5 validation — it must be duplicated server-side; client validation is UX-only
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how :invalid/:valid CSS and the Constraint Validation API (setCustomValidity) let you customize error UX

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **HTML5 Input Types & Validation Attributes — Complete Reference** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** What HTML5 input types and validation attributes are available? Give examples.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Input types (email, url, number, tel, date, color, range, search, file) and attributes (required, pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength)**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Relying solely on HTML5 validation — it must be duplicated server-side; client validation is UX-only**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Show how :invalid/:valid CSS and the Constraint Validation API (setCustomValidity) let you customize error UX**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Input types (email, url, number, tel, date, color, range, search, file) and attributes (required, pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength)
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **relying solely on HTML5 validation — it must be duplicated server-side; client validation is UX-only** and what you do instead.

questions.question: How do you make HTML forms accessible?
questions.title: Accessible HTML Forms — Labels, Fieldsets, Error Announcements
questions.direct_answer:
How do you make HTML forms accessible?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser pipeline, framework hooks, and user-visible outcomes), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Explicit label associations (for/id or wrapping), fieldset/legend for groups, aria-invalid/aria-describedby for errors, focus management.

**Classic weak answer:** Relying on placeholder text as the only label — fails screen readers and disappears when typing.

**Senior finish:** Show a complete accessible form with error summary, live-region announcements, and keyboard focus on first invalid field.

interviewer_intent.testing: Explicit label associations (for/id or wrapping), fieldset/legend for groups, aria-invalid/aria-describedby for errors, focus management
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying on placeholder text as the only label — fails screen readers and disappears when typing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete accessible form with error summary, live-region announcements, and keyboard focus on first invalid field
